explained_behaviors.summary: Turning after or attacking its own tail. Common play in kittens; new or intense tail chasing in an adult cat has several medical differentials.
explained_behaviors.temporal_notes: In kittens bouts are short and playful, interleaved with other play; episodic bouts with skin rippling and running off point elsewhere.

play_or_normal.explanation: predatory play with the tail as a moving target, typical of kittens and playful young cats

medical.explanation: itch or skin disease at the tail base (fleas, allergy, other dermatitis) - one reason a cat turns to bite or lick the tail
pain in the tail, the lower back or the anal sacs

feline hyperaesthesia syndrome: brief episodes with rippling skin over the lower back, dilated pupils, tail chasing or biting, sudden running and sometimes vocalizing - a diagnosis made after other causes are excluded
focal seizures, when episodes are abrupt, stereotyped and cannot be interrupted
circling that is not tail chasing: tight circles always in the same direction, often with a head tilt or loss of balance, point to a balance (vestibular) or brain problem

arousal_or_stress.explanation: stress or conflict (a household change, other pets); it can add to the episodes but is not shown to cause them

explained_behaviors.no_request_note: No request or intention is implied by this behaviour itself.

explained_behaviors.summary: Scratching the body or ears with a hind foot.

medical.explanation: itch from parasites, allergy or ear disease when it is frequent or focused

play_or_normal.explanation: occasional scratching is ordinary coat care

explained_behaviors.no_request_note: No request or intention is implied by this behaviour itself.

uncertainty: The recording can show what the animal does and when; it cannot establish why. Candidate explanations come from the cited sources, ordered by how well your description matches them.
Behaviour recognition uses a general vision-language model (zero-shot); scores are relative, not probabilities, and its measured accuracy is in results/e31.
Context taken from the recording (people, objects, sounds, place) comes from automatic detectors and can be wrong; it changes the order of the candidates only half as much as your description.
observations_needed: How old is the cat, and is the tail chasing new or has it done this since kittenhood?
Does the skin on the lower back ripple or twitch, or do the pupils dilate, during an episode? Does the cat run off afterwards?
Does the cat react when you touch the base of the tail or the lower back?
Is there hair loss, scabs, flea dirt or a wound on the tail or near its base?
Can you interrupt an episode (call, toy), and how long does it last?
Does it always circle in the same direction, with a head tilt or loss of balance?
Is it frequent or focused on one place (ears, neck)?
Are there fleas, flea dirt, redness or discharge from the ears?
urgent_signs: the tail is wounded, bleeding or the cat keeps attacking it
episodes with unresponsiveness, drooling or loss of bladder control
a sudden new behaviour in an adult or senior cat
circling with a head tilt, falling or loss of balance
bleeding or open sores from scratching

sources.citation: Merrimack River Feline Rescue Society, Ask a Vet: Why do cats chase their tails?
sources.supports: tail chasing is common play and hunting practice in kittens; a new behaviour in an adult cat should be checked by a veterinarian

sources.citation: Ellis SLH et al. (2013) AAFP and ISFM feline environmental needs guidelines. J Feline Med Surg 15:219-230 (as summarized by Veterinary Partner).
sources.supports: cats need opportunities for play and predatory behaviour and predictable interactions with people

sources.citation: Amengual Batle P et al. (2019) Feline hyperaesthesia syndrome with self-trauma to the tail: retrospective study of seven cases. J Feline Med Surg 21(2).
sources.supports: tail chasing and self-trauma in young cats; hypersensitivity dermatitis suspected in some; fleas should be eliminated even in indoor cats

sources.citation: Today's Veterinary Practice: Answering FAQs about feline hyperesthesia syndrome.
sources.supports: diagnosis of exclusion; consider skin disease and spinal, tail and anal-sac pain; consider focal seizures when episodes are stereotyped, abrupt and not interruptible; many signs also occur in healthy cats
itch is the most common sign of skin disease and leads to scratching, licking and biting; behavioural causes link to stress, frustration or conflict; diagnosis of exclusion

sources.citation: Cornell Feline Health Center: Hyperesthesia syndrome.
sources.supports: skin sensitivity near the base of the tail; scratching, biting, tail chasing, dilated pupils, rippling skin; underlying causes (for example disc disease) must be evaluated; stress adds to the reaction

sources.citation: A presumptive diagnosis of feline hyperesthesia syndrome due to stressful human-related condition: case report. Vet Res Commun (2026).
sources.supports: tail chasing and lumbar tremors began after a household change (birth of a child); the authors state that a causal relationship cannot be established

sources.citation: Merck Veterinary Manual: The neurologic examination of animals.
sources.supports: a head tilt usually indicates vestibular dysfunction; animals with forebrain lesions may turn their heads and circle in one direction

sources.citation: dvm360: Vestibular disease in dogs and cats (proceedings).
sources.supports: vestibular disorders cause head tilt, falling, rolling, leaning, circling and abnormal eye movements; circling also occurs with focal forebrain lesions

sources.citation: Veterinary Partner (VIN): Vestibular disease in dogs and cats.
sources.supports: middle- and inner-ear problems are separate from brain problems; localizing the cause decides outlook and treatment

sources.citation: Waisglass SE et al. (2006) Underlying medical conditions in cats with presumptive psychogenic alopecia. J Am Vet Med Assoc 228(11):1705-1709.
sources.supports: of 21 overgrooming cats presumed psychogenic, 16 had a medical cause of itch, 3 both, 2 a purely behavioural cause

answer.summary: In the recording: turning in tight circles (after its own tail or not) (2.0-6.0 s, 10.0-14.5 s, 19.5-25.0 s, 35.0-39.0 s); scratching its own body with a hind foot (0.0-2.5 s, 5.5-6.5 s, 8.5-9.0 s). Turning in tight circles (after its own tail or not) (recording) has several possible explanations, in order of fit to your description: ordinary play or maintenance behaviour; discomfort, itch, pain or a neurological cause; arousal, frustration or stress. No request is implied by it. Scratching its own body with a hind foot (recording) has several possible explanations, in order of fit to your description: discomfort, itch, pain or a neurological cause; ordinary play or maintenance behaviour.
